text: Before our school trip, Mira showed me a picture of Earth. ‘The atmosphere is the air around us; the hydrosphere includes all water; the lithosphere is Earth’s hard outer layer,’ she said. Below the crust lay the mantle and core. We learned that water contains hydrogen and oxygen, and that carbon dioxide helps keep Earth warm through the greenhouse effect. Then we checked our map’s longitude and latitude. Our camp was at a high altitude. I looked toward the horizon and smiled. Today, the words in my notebook would become part of a real adventure.

Mira led us through changing terrain. The landscape was like a tiny continent: a cave opened below a cliff, a glacier shone far above us, and a river ran toward a swamp and a delta. I picked up a pebble. ‘Is this valuable ore?’ I asked. Mira held a magnet near it. ‘One test is not enough,’ she said. At camp, we used a mineral chart to compare quartz, granite and marble. A red mark on another rock was iron oxide. Suddenly, even a small stone had a story to tell.

That afternoon, a gentle breeze became a sudden gust. Soon a gale shook our tent. Rain arrived with the monsoon. On the radio, a teacher explained El Niño, a phenomenon that can change rain patterns. She also described a hurricane, a typhoon and a tornado; these were things to learn about, not names for every strong wind. Outside, mist hid the trees. Far away, a factory began to fume, adding to the smog. We stayed inside, waiting for the rain to stop.

Our radio then reported seismic activity near a volcano. An earthquake might make it unsafe to stay. Scientists were studying magma with a thermodynamic model, but nobody knew whether the volcano would erupt. We followed the teachers to a safe building. There, a poster showed how a tsunami, an avalanche, a drought or flooding could become a disaster. A torrent outside reminded us that water could be destructive. I dropped my bag: a small mishap, not a calamity. ‘Ignoring warnings could endanger everyone and jeopardise our return,’ Mira said. ‘A careless choice can have catastrophic results.’ When we finally got home, I opened my notebook. Now I could remember every word through our trip.

After our first trip, Mira invited me to a camp in Oceania. On a globe, she showed me the equator, a hemisphere and each pole. Earth turns around its axis. Pictures of Arctic ice and an Antarctic station helped us understand the polar regions. Our route crossed the Atlantic and the Pacific Ocean; another photograph showed the Mediterranean Sea. ‘Every place has its own story,’ she said. I remembered the longitude and latitude from our first lesson. This time, we would help a village find its missing water.

Our navigation system guided us into a gulf beside a peninsula. The mainland lay nearby. A marine research team met us on the coast. We walked from a sandy beach to a stony shore, watching the tide and current. A brook once joined a shallow stream here, but now both were almost dry. We followed the old path toward the source. The flat ground became rough, then steep. A smooth pebble lay beside a nearly vertical wall. Two parallel tracks crossed a narrow bridge. Somewhere above us, the water had stopped.

Beyond a plain, we climbed a plateau and found a tiny oasis. ‘A superficial inspection will not explain this,’ Mira warned. The village’s water system needed an upgrade. Broken pipes could make conditions deteriorate, aggravate shortages and degrade the land. Heavy rain could also erode the exposed ground. We found a blocked pipe and called the team. While waiting, I opened our meteorology notebook. Climate describes long-term patterns; weather tells us what happens today. A single dry afternoon could not explain the whole problem.

Our camp stood near the Tropic of Capricorn. The days were warm and humid, but the higher ground was mild, with more moderate temperatures. One side of the plateau was arid; the other had moist soil and damp stones. Far above, a snowy peak still carried frost. At night, we used heating and thermal blankets. By morning, the team had repaired the pipe. Water returned to the brook. The village had not needed a miracle: it had needed careful observation and a practical repair.

Our next trip began on a stormy morning. Thunder followed lightning, and a shower became a downpour. Hail struck the window. The forecast predicted heavy rainfall and a temperature near zero degrees Celsius. Outside, a frigid wind brought a chill. I began to shiver, and my hands would tremble whenever I tried to write. Water could freeze overnight, then thaw during the day. By afternoon, only a sprinkle remained, and a rainbow appeared. We waited for our teacher to say the path was safe.

We climbed a mountain called Mount Echo. From its peak, a long range stretched into the distance. A ridge above the slope allowed us to overlook the valley. On the eastern hillside grew oriental lilies. A village lay to the southeast, a farm to the southwest, and a forest to the northeast. The northwest was hidden by clouds. In the southern part of the valley, a stream looked brown. ‘Do not overlook that colour,’ Mira said. Our trip suddenly had a question to answer.

We left a suburb, passed the outskirts of town and reached a rural road. A remote house stood in a desolate field, below a distant cliff. Adjacent to it was an old workshop. At the border of the field, a broken metal plate covered a pipe. Along the fringe of the grass lay clay and dirt. Muddy water carried silt and sediment toward the stream. Mira drew the pipe in the margin of our map. A lesson in geology had become a search for evidence.

The pipe leaked irregularly. This abnormal flow might carry a toxic pollutant and contaminate the water. We reported the possible pollution instead of touching it. ‘Guessing would be inappropriate,’ our teacher said. ‘We need samples.’ A serious disaster was not inevitable, but some damage could be irreversible. The village closed the pipe while experts checked it. That evening, I wrote two notes: observe carefully, and act before a small problem becomes a large one. Our muddy shoes were a small price for a useful lesson.

At sunrise, we entered an old garden beside the wilderness. Debris covered the path, and a crack left a gap in the wall. ‘This could be a splendid place,’ Mira said. A grand tree stood above a magnificent stone arch. Our teacher called the project a super idea and an interesting challenge. The change would be dramatic. Nearby, a desert was spreading. If people continued to deforest the hills, more land could become barren. We wanted fertile soil, so we would fertilise carefully and plant new trees.

A spring once fed a fountain and a little waterfall. Now the reservoir was nearly empty. We watched water drip from a broken pipe, pour into a drain and gush through a hole. In the sunshine, water could evaporate into vapour; water and air would circulate through the garden. Dew appeared on cool leaves at dawn. In a small laboratory test, dissolved substances began to precipitate as solids. We learned to check water quality, not simply admire clear water. Clean water was the garden’s first need.

A puff of smoke rose from a machine. The wind began to blow it away. We compared petrol and gasoline and learned that they name the same fuel; gas can also mean a gaseous fuel. We chose an electric tool instead. After intensive work, the surrounding area was in better condition. The situation improved, but dense clouds made us watch the storm’s intensity. We saw a warning light flash and a worker emerge from the shed. Near deep water, life jackets could help people float rather than drown. Safety came before speed.

At sunset, we rested in the shade and watched a tree’s shadow stretch across the path. At dusk, the garden felt like heaven, a small paradise for everyone. Our calendar marked a future lunar eclipse; Mira also hoped to see a solar eclipse one day. We discussed the environment and our place in nature. Natural stone paths could sit beside an artificial pond, but we would keep synthetic waste out of the water. The garden was not finished. Still, its new beginning gave us a reason to return.

For our final task, Mira and I wrote a letter to our future selves. We drew the atmosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere, then marked our village’s longitude and latitude. Beyond a plain stood a plateau where our first adventure had begun. ‘Weather changes every day,’ I wrote, ‘but climate describes patterns over many years.’ A chill made me shiver. My hands began to tremble, so we moved inside to finish the letter.

Our last new word was petroleum: oil found underground and used to make fuels and other products. A leak could release a toxic pollutant and contaminate water. It could endanger animals and jeopardise people’s lives. ‘Do not let a small problem deteriorate,’ Mira wrote. ‘Careless actions can aggravate it and degrade the land.’ If we deforest a hillside, rain may erode its soil. These were no longer separate words. They described choices that people make every day.

We promised to protect fertile soil and fertilise carefully. Beside an artificial pond, we would remove synthetic waste and plant trees. One day, children could rest in their shade and watch each shadow move across the path. Damage was not inevitable, although some harm could be irreversible. We closed the letter and opened our notebooks again. This time, we covered the English words and tried to tell the whole story from memory. The words we could not remember would be tomorrow’s first review.
